findings.quote: metformin, DOACs and many antibiotics are dosed by eGFR
findings.explanation: Dosing and contraindication thresholds for direct oral anticoagulants in UK SmPCs, the BNF and MHRA advice are based on creatinine clearance estimated with the Cockcroft-Gault equation (which uses weight), not on eGFR. Metformin and many antibiotics are dosed by eGFR; DOACs are the well-known exception, and eGFR can mislead in older, frail or very light or heavy people.
findings.suggestedFix: Write 'metformin and many antibiotics are dosed by eGFR; DOACs are dosed by creatinine clearance (Cockcroft-Gault)', or simply say the doses depend on kidney function.

findings.quote: growth within 48 hours confirms bloodstream infection and its organism
findings.explanation: Growth in a blood-culture bottle does not by itself confirm infection: skin contaminants grow too, which the same page says in interpretation[1] ('Skin organism in one bottle only: probably contamination'). Whether it is true bacteraemia depends on the organism, how many sets are positive and the clinical picture. The same sentence also says 'Two bottles from separate sites'; the standard is two sets (one aerobic and one anaerobic bottle each) from separate venepunctures, as the later 'more than one set' implies.
findings.suggestedFix: Say growth is the first sign of possible bloodstream infection, that the organism, growth in more than one set and the clinical picture decide whether it is real, and use 'two sets from separate sites'. Keep a timing statement soft (most true positives flag within a day or two, but incubation continues for several days).

findings.explanation: Numeric bands appear in prose ('above 100 mg/L' here, 'roughly 5-20 mg/L' in interpretation[1]) with no thresholds record and no source, while rangePolicy is 'laboratory' and rangeNote says 'There is no diagnostic threshold'. The prose therefore contradicts the entity's own range policy (and the sister biomarker entry, which tells readers to use the laboratory's printed interval). The only widely used UK cut-offs near these figures are in NICE point-of-care CRP advice for chest infection (about 20 and 100 mg/L), a different purpose; the cited MedlinePlus and Lab Tests Online pages do not give them. Units are mg/L (UK/EU style), which is fine.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace the bands with 'markedly raised' and 'mildly raised', or add thresholds records with a named UK source and jurisdiction and amend rangeNote to match.

findings.quote: differ slightly between countries and professional bodies
findings.explanation: rangePolicy is 'threshold' and interpretation uses Deficient / Insufficient / Adequate, yet the entity has no thresholds records, no cut-off values and no unit, so the categories are undefined. 'Differ slightly' also understates the gap: UK practice (Royal Osteoporosis Society, NICE CKS) treats under 25 nmol/L as deficient and over 50 nmol/L as sufficient, whereas the US Endocrine Society used under 50 nmol/L (20 ng/mL) for deficiency, and the units differ (nmol/L vs ng/mL, factor 2.5). The sister entry biomarkers/vitamin-d-25-oh says some guidelines no longer endorse fixed thresholds, which also conflicts with rangePolicy 'threshold'.
findings.suggestedFix: Either add thresholds records with a UK source, nmol/L and jurisdiction (and say US cut-offs differ), or set rangePolicy to 'laboratory' and write 'the cut-offs differ between countries and bodies; the report states the ones used'. Drop 'slightly'.

findings.quote: Self-tests carry the same window-period limits and need confirmation.
findings.explanation: The page gives about 45 days only for the fourth-generation laboratory test. Most rapid finger-prick and saliva or home self-test kits detect antibody only (a few newer kits add antigen) and, in UK guidance, need about 90 days (3 months) after exposure for a reliable negative. 'The same window-period limits' reads as equal and could falsely reassure someone who tests negative at six weeks; it also sits badly with factors[0] ('depends on the test type').
findings.suggestedFix: State that antibody-only rapid and self-tests have a longer window period (usually about 90 days in UK guidance), so an early negative needs repeating, and that a reactive result needs laboratory confirmation.

findings.quote: After a possible exposure, at the right interval
findings.explanation: The page tells people with a possible exposure to test 'at the right interval' and to repeat later (preparation, interpretation), but never says that post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is time-critical: it works best started within hours and no later than 72 hours, and is obtained through a sexual health clinic or A&E, not by waiting for a test. A search of the content finds no PEP signposting anywhere, so a reader could wait out the window period and lose the chance of PEP.
findings.suggestedFix: Add one sentence: after a possible high-risk exposure, seek urgent advice (sexual health clinic, A&E or NHS 111) about PEP, which must start within 72 hours; testing at the window period is separate.

findings.quote: treatment considered if TSH stays above 10 mU/L or with symptoms, pregnancy or planning pregnancy
findings.explanation: The prose says 'above 10 mU/L' but the entity's own threshold record (and NICE NG145) says 10 or above on two occasions three months apart, so a TSH of exactly 10 is classed differently in the two places. The prose also loses the two-occasions-three-months-apart condition and the NICE nuance that, below 10, a time-limited levothyroxine trial is considered mainly in symptomatic adults under 65.
findings.suggestedFix: Use 'persistently 10 mU/L or higher' to match the record.

findings.quote: NT-proBNP below 400 ng/L (or BNP below 100 ng/L) in an untreated person
findings.explanation: The BNP cut-off of 100 ng/L has no thresholds record (all three records are NT-proBNP only), although rangeNote says the BNP and NT-proBNP thresholds differ and the page cites NICE NG106, which, to my knowledge, gives its referral bands for NT-proBNP only. The BNP figure appears to come from older NICE guidance or US practice, so its source and jurisdiction are not stated.
findings.suggestedFix: Remove the BNP figure, or add a BNP threshold record with a named source and jurisdiction.

findings.quote: Significant bacterial infection or major inflammation until proven otherwise
findings.explanation: Overreaches and conflicts with the page's own limitations ('the overlap between the two is considerable') and cannotTell ('Whether an infection is bacterial or viral with certainty'). A CRP above 100 mg/L also occurs with some viral infections (adenovirus, influenza, COVID-19), after surgery or trauma, with infarction and in flares of inflammatory disease.
findings.suggestedFix: 'Marked inflammation; bacterial infection is a common cause but the level does not prove it, so the source is sought with examination, imaging and cultures'.

findings.explanation: A numeric cut-off in prose with no thresholds record or source; rangePolicy is 'laboratory' and rangeNote says limits depend on age and sex and that laboratories publish their own. The figure is conventional but is not supported by the two cited pages (a MedlinePlus patient page and a PMC reference-interval paper) and conflicts with the 'use the laboratory interval' policy.
findings.suggestedFix: Say 'markedly raised ESR' without a number, or add a threshold record with a source.

findings.quote: Expected; a rise above about 30% prompts review of the dose and a search for renal artery narrowing
findings.explanation: A numeric action threshold in prose with no thresholds record, and the cited NG203 section (1.1 Investigations) is not where ACE inhibitor/ARB monitoring sits. As I recall NICE advice, creatinine rise of 30% or more or eGFR fall of 25% or more from baseline prompts a search for other causes first (volume depletion, NSAIDs) and then dose reduction or stopping; 'above about 30%' leaves out the eGFR criterion and the first step, though renal artery stenosis is a legitimate further consideration.
findings.suggestedFix: Soften to 'a larger rise prompts review of the dose and a search for causes such as dehydration, NSAIDs or renal artery narrowing', or add a threshold record with the correct NICE section.

findings.quote: readings are repeated and the average used
findings.explanation: The page's UK threshold source (NICE NG136) says that if the first clinic reading is 140/90 or higher a second is taken, a third if they differ substantially, and the lower of the last two is recorded as the clinic blood pressure. Averaging repeated clinic readings is ESC/US practice; presented as general it does not match the UK method the thresholds assume.
findings.suggestedFix: 'a second (and if needed third) reading is taken and, in UK practice, the lower of the last two is recorded'; keep 'averaged' for home and ambulatory readings.

findings.quote: Very early or 'window period' infection, when only anti-HBc IgM may be positive
findings.explanation: 'Only anti-HBc (IgM) positive' describes the core window late in acute infection, after HBsAg has cleared and before anti-HBs appears. Very early infection shows HBsAg and/or HBV DNA first, and anti-HBc IgM comes later, so 'very early' is wrong for this pattern.
findings.suggestedFix: 'The core-antibody window late in acute infection, when HBsAg has cleared but anti-HBs has not yet appeared and only anti-HBc IgM may be positive; in the first weeks HBsAg or HBV DNA appears first'.

findings.quote: depends on factors VII, X, V, II and fibrinogen, the factors warfarin and liver disease reduce
findings.explanation: Reads as if warfarin reduces all five. Warfarin lowers only the vitamin K-dependent factors (II, VII, IX, X); factor V and fibrinogen are not vitamin K-dependent and are not reduced by warfarin, although severe liver disease lowers them.
findings.suggestedFix: 'depends on factors VII, X, V, II and fibrinogen; warfarin lowers the vitamin K-dependent ones (II, VII, X), while liver disease can lower all of them'.

findings.quote: NICE TA464: Bisphosphonates for treating osteoporosis
findings.explanation: Title and URL agree, but a technology appraisal of bisphosphonates does not support anything this page says about vitamin D testing, cut-offs, interpretation or the statement that population screening is not recommended. No cited source covers vitamin D thresholds or testing policy.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace with a UK source on vitamin D testing and cut-offs (for example NICE CKS on vitamin D deficiency in adults, or Royal Osteoporosis Society guidance), or remove.

findings.explanation: The page is about serum iron, TIBC, transferrin saturation and the patterns across them (components, interpretation, factors), but none of the three references covers those tests: an NHS anaemia page, a ferritin test page and a haemoglobin test page. The haemoglobin page is the least relevant.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a source that covers serum iron, TIBC and transferrin saturation (for example a MedlinePlus iron tests page or a UK pathology or NICE CKS source) and drop the haemoglobin page.

findings.quote: Abdominal pain, black or dark stools, vomiting or fever after the procedure are reasons to contact the unit promptly.
findings.explanation: Warning signs are listed, but there is no route for severe or out-of-hours problems (perforation and heavy bleeding are emergencies) and no after-sedation precautions (no driving, alcohol or signing legal documents for 24 hours; an adult to take the person home). These are standard in sedated-endoscopy patient information and bear on safety; the page describes recovery without them.
findings.suggestedFix: Add that severe pain, heavy bleeding, vomiting blood, chest pain, breathlessness or fever need urgent help (the unit, or A&E/999 out of hours), and that after sedation people should not drive, drink alcohol or sign legal documents for 24 hours and should have someone with them.

findings.quote: The INR is only meaningful for vitamin K antagonists such as warfarin
findings.explanation: Read literally this conflicts with the rest of the page, which uses PT/INR for liver synthetic function, vitamin K deficiency and DIC (whyOrdered, components, interpretation). The INR is calibrated and validated for warfarin monitoring, but it is widely used as a marker in liver disease with reagent-dependent caveats.
findings.suggestedFix: 'The INR is calibrated for warfarin monitoring; in liver disease it is used as a marker of synthetic function but varies with the reagent and does not measure bleeding risk; direct oral anticoagulants prolong it unpredictably and need different tests'.

notes: All 19 entities read in full; 18 findings, none of high severity. No web access, so URLs were judged only on title versus slug; unverifiable offline and not flagged: the MedlinePlus ency article 002360 titled 'Endoscope' (endoscopy), the BNP and eGFR MedlinePlus slugs, and the gov.uk trans-screening slug ('transgender-people') versus its title ('trans and non-binary people'). Borderline items deliberately not reported: microbiology 'Cultures are negative in a third of sepsis cases' (defensible for cultures from any site, but blood cultures alone are positive in only about a third of sepsis cases and the cited pages give no figure); cervical-screening 'intervals that depend on age' may be out of date if England's move to 5-yearly recall for HPV-negative 25-49 year olds (2025, date not certain) applies; TSH monitoring '6-8 weeks' (NICE NG145 says every 3 months until stable, then yearly) and biotin 'paused for two days' are unsourced; prothrombin-time-inr medicinesNote lists NSAIDs as raising the INR (they mainly add bleeding risk, a few such as piroxicam do raise INR); troponin alias 'cardiac enzymes' (troponin is not an enzyme); biopsy 'a punch or shave that removes the top layers' (a punch biopsy is full thickness) and PD-L1 listed under 'targeted treatment' (it guides immunotherapy); vitamin-b12-folate whyOrdered 'Before and during pregnancy planning, for folate' (routine folate testing is not UK practice; supplementation advice is universal). Cross-file points: biomarkers/vitamin-d-25-oh says some guidelines no longer endorse fixed thresholds (conflicts with tests/vitamin-d rangePolicy 'threshold'), and biomarkers/crp, bnp, tsh and ferritin tell readers to use the laboratory interval rather than quoted figures, which sits oddly with numeric bands in the CRP, ESR and BNP test prose. The first four entities (endoscopy, biopsy, genetic-testing, microbiology-tests) use an older schema with no rangePolicy or review block. Anatomy and condition tags look auto-generated and some are odd (hiv-test lists sepsis, pneumonia and thymus; crp lists 'Caudate lobe of liver'); they were not treated as claims.
